title: Random forests
story:
A single deep tree has a specific pathology: it is close to exact on the data it was built from and violently unstable off it. Change a handful of rows, an early split flips, and everything beneath that split is a different tree with different predictions. The method has low bias and enormous variance, and variance is the failure that a held-out score reveals late.

The remedy is to average, but averaging only helps if the things being averaged make different mistakes. Average a thousand trees grown the same way on the same data and you get one tree back, because they are all the same tree. So the trick is to force disagreement deliberately. Breiman's definition in 2001 is a combination of tree predictors where each tree depends on the values of a random vector sampled independently and with the same distribution for all trees in the forest — the randomness is the design, not an implementation detail. In practice it enters twice: each tree sees a resample of the rows, and at each node it is allowed to consider only a random subset of the features.

The second of those is the one that does the real work and it is worth understanding why. Resampling alone leaves the trees highly correlated, because one dominant feature will be chosen at the root of nearly every tree and the structure beneath will be similar. Restricting the features available at each node forces trees to be built around the second- and third-best variables sometimes, which produces genuinely different trees — including ones that discover structure the greedy path in a single tree would never have reached.

The result that makes this more than a heuristic is Breiman's convergence statement: the generalisation error converges almost surely to a limit as the number of trees becomes large, and that limit depends on two quantities, the strength of the individual trees and the correlation between them. Read what it implies. Adding trees moves you toward a limit rather than away from one, so more trees do not make the forest worse — the usual worry about adding capacity does not apply in this direction. And the limit itself is governed by a tension: anything you do to make the trees more different from one another tends to make each one weaker, and the best setting is wherever that trade bottoms out.

What you give up is legibility. A single tree is a readable sequence of conditions; five hundred averaged trees are not a rule anyone can state. That is a real loss, and it is the reason the next lesson on feature importance exists at all — importance measures are the attempt to recover some of what averaging destroyed.

problem.name: Bagged randomised ensembles
problem.shape: A model class fits its training data very closely and gives quite different answers when the training data changes slightly.
tell: small changes to the data produce very different models
training error is near zero and held-out error is not
the base model is unstable but roughly unbiased
one feature dominates the top of every tree
problem.move: Grow many of the unstable models and average them, and make them disagree on purpose — resample the rows for each, and restrict each split to a random subset of the features. Add trees freely, since the error converges rather than degrading, and tune the feature-subset size, which is what sets the trade between individual strength and mutual correlation.
problem.invariant: The generalisation error converges almost surely to a limit as the number of trees grows, and that limit is set by the strength of the individual trees and by the correlation between them.
problem.breaks: Averaging reduces variance and does nothing to shared bias. If every tree is wrong in the same direction — because the feature the problem needs is absent, or because the axis-aligned form cannot express the boundary — then a thousand of them are wrong in that direction too, and the stability of the answer is no evidence for it.

cost.time: linear in the number of trees for both fitting and prediction, though the trees are independent and so embarrassingly parallel
cost.space: every tree is retained, so the model is orders of magnitude larger than one tree and is no longer readable
cost.beats: a single tuned tree, which is legible and unstable, and heavy pruning, which buys stability by giving up the fit

worked.problem: Why does adding more trees to a forest not make it overfit?
worked.reasoning:
Because adding trees is not adding capacity in the sense that causes overfitting. It is averaging more samples from a fixed distribution of models, and the result converges.

The precise statement is that the generalisation error converges almost surely to a limit as the number of trees becomes large. That is a convergence result, not a bound that degrades: each additional tree moves the average closer to the expected prediction of the randomised procedure, and once you are near that limit further trees change very little. There is no mechanism by which the thousandth tree makes the forest worse than the five-hundredth, so the number of trees is a computational budget rather than a hyper-parameter to be tuned against a validation set.

That is genuinely different from most of what this track contains, and it is worth being clear about why, because the intuition that more model means more overfitting is usually right. The difference is that the trees are not fitted jointly against a single objective. Each is grown independently on its own resample; none of them sees what the others did or corrects for it. So the ensemble is an estimate of an average, and adding terms to an average reduces its variance rather than increasing its fit.

What does overfit is the individual tree, and that is controlled separately by depth or leaf size. A forest of fully grown trees can still have a limit that is worse than it needs to be — it just will not get worse as you add more of them.

The limit is governed by the two quantities in the result: the strength of the individual trees and the correlation between them. That is where the actual tuning lives. Restricting the number of features considered at each split makes trees more different from one another, which lowers correlation and helps, but also makes each tree weaker, which hurts. The best setting is wherever that trade bottoms out, and it is the parameter worth spending effort on.

The important contrast I would draw is with boosting, where the same question has the opposite answer. There the models are fitted in sequence, each to the errors of those before it, so they are not independent samples of anything and adding stages does eventually overfit. In a forest, the number of trees is a budget; in boosting, it is a parameter.

problem.practice: Fit a forest and plot held-out error against the number of trees, out to several hundred. Confirm the curve flattens rather than turning upward. Then hold the tree count fixed and vary the number of features considered per split, and watch the error move — that is the parameter that changes the limit.

beats.broke: A single deep tree fits its training data almost exactly, and a small change to that data produces an entirely different tree — accurate in sample and unstable out of it.
beats.fix: Grow many trees, each on a resample and each choosing splits from a random subset of features, then average them. The randomisation exists to make the trees disagree, because averaging models that agree buys nothing.
beats.cost: The averaged model is no longer a rule anyone can read, and the remaining error is set by a trade between how strong the individual trees are and how correlated they remain.

interview.q: Why does adding more trees to a forest not make it overfit?
interview.trap: Appealing to averaging in general. The reason is specific: the trees are fitted independently rather than jointly, so the ensemble estimates an average and the generalisation error converges to a limit — which is exactly why boosting, where models are fitted in sequence, answers this question the other way.
interview.answer:
Because adding trees is not adding capacity in the sense that causes overfitting — it is averaging more samples from a fixed distribution of models, and the result converges.

The precise statement is that the generalisation error converges almost surely to a limit as the number of trees becomes large. Each additional tree moves the average closer to the expected prediction of the randomised procedure, and near that limit further trees change little. There is no mechanism by which the thousandth tree makes the forest worse than the five-hundredth, so the tree count is a computational budget rather than something to tune against a validation set.

That differs from most of this track, and the reason matters, because the intuition that more model means more overfitting is usually correct. The difference is that these trees are not fitted jointly against one objective. Each is grown independently on its own resample and never sees what the others did, so the ensemble is an estimate of an average — and adding terms to an average reduces its variance rather than increasing its fit.

What does overfit is the individual tree, controlled separately by depth or leaf size. A forest of fully grown trees can have a worse limit than necessary; it simply will not get worse as trees are added.

The limit is set by the two quantities in the result: individual strength and inter-tree correlation. That is where tuning actually lives. Restricting features per split makes trees more different, lowering correlation, but also makes each weaker — the best setting is where that trade bottoms out.

The contrast worth drawing is with boosting, where the same question has the opposite answer: there the models are fitted in sequence to each other's errors, so they are not independent samples and adding stages does eventually overfit.

ONE DEEP TREE

   low bias, ENORMOUS variance
   flip an early split -> a different model

AVERAGE, BUT MAKE THEM DISAGREE

   resample the ROWS        (weaker effect)
   random FEATURE SUBSET    (the real work)
      per node

   without the second: one dominant feature sits
   at every root, trees stay correlated, and
   averaging buys little.

THE CONVERGENCE RESULT

   error -> a LIMIT, almost surely, as trees grow

   limit = f( strength of each tree,
              correlation between them )

SO:

   tree count      a COMPUTE BUDGET
                   (more never hurts)
   depth/leaf size what actually controls
                   individual overfitting
   features/split  what moves the LIMIT
                   fewer -> less correlated,
                            weaker trees

WHY IT CANNOT OVERFIT BY COUNT

   trees are fitted INDEPENDENTLY, not jointly.
   the ensemble estimates an AVERAGE.
   more terms -> lower variance of that estimate.

WHAT AVERAGING CANNOT FIX

   shared BIAS.
   all axis-aligned -> all approximate the same
   diagonal with the same staircase.
   1000 wrong in one direction is still wrong,
   and now it is STABLE, which looks like
   confidence.

WHAT IT COSTS

   legibility. 500 trees are not a rule.
   -> which is why feature importance exists.
takeaway: A forest works by forcing its trees to disagree, and its error converges to a limit set by their individual strength against their mutual correlation — so more trees are a budget rather than a risk, while shared bias survives any amount of averaging.
